security_spec.violation_condition: In ChiselIOPMP's Ctrl module (IopmpChecker.scala:1238-1239), when constructing the NAPOT entry address for the NAPOTDecoder, the hardware hardcodes the lower 2 bits as 2'b11 via `Cat(io.entry.addr, 3.U(2.W))`. This assumes a fixed granularity that ignores the configurable G field. Per the spec fix: when granularity G>=2 and the mode is NAPOT, entry address bits [G-2:0] must read as all ones. The Chisel implementation does not reference any granularity register to compute the number of lower bits that should be forced to 1. If G > 2, bits beyond [1:0] that should be all-ones per the spec are left at their raw entry_addr values (which may be zero), causing the NAPOT decoder to compute an incorrectly smaller address range — start address shifted downward relative to spec, end address correspondingly smaller. This causes incorrect address matching: transactions to addresses within the spec-defined NAPOT range but outside the incorrectly-computed range will fail to match, resulting in spurious access denials (function loss / denial of service).
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: Cat(io.entry.addr, 3.U(2.W)) NAPOT entry_addr construction without granularity G mask; HWCFG0 granularity field not consulted before NAPOT address decode
security_spec.summary: ChiselIOPMP NAPOT address construction hardcodes lower 2 bits as 2'b11 instead of replicating ones across bits [G-2:0] per hardware granularity G, causing incorrect NAPOT range computation when G > 2

location.function_name: Ctrl FSM — sPriority state, entry_addr construction for NAPOT mode

findings.finding: NAPOT entry_addr pads exactly 2 lower bits (3.U(2.W) = 2'b11) via Cat(io.entry.addr, 3.U(2.W)). No granularity G register is consulted. Per spec, when G>=2 and mode is NAPOT, bits [G-2:0] must read as all-ones. For G>2, bits [G-2:2] are left at their raw io.entry.addr values (possibly zero), causing NAPOTDecoder to compute an incorrectly smaller address range. Transactions within the spec-defined NAPOT range but outside the incorrectly-computed range fail to match, producing spurious access denials (DoS).

location.function_name: Ctrl FSM — sPriority state, entry_addr wire declaration

findings.finding: entry_addr wire is declared as UInt(IopmpParams.soc_addr_width.W) = 48 bits (soc_addr_width=48 at line 116), but io.entry.addr is 64 bits (EntryTableIO line 359). Cat(io.entry.addr, 3.U(2.W)) produces 66 bits. Assigning 66 bits to a 48-bit wire silently truncates the upper 18 bits — including most of entry_addrh (the high 32 bits of the 64-bit programmed entry address). The entry_addrh data is effectively discarded for NAPOT/NA4 decode, causing address matching against truncated addresses that do not reflect programmed upper-address bits.

location.function_name: Ctrl FSM — sPriority state, entry_addr construction for NA4 mode

findings.finding: Same granularity bug affects NA4 mode: Cat(io.entry.addr, 1.U(2.W)) hardcodes exactly 2 lower bits (2'b01) without consulting granularity G. Per spec, when G>=2 and mode is NA4, entry address bits [G-2:0] must read as 00...01 (G-2 zeros followed by a one). For G>2, bits [G-2:2] are left at raw values instead of being forced to zero, causing the NA4 decoder to compute an incorrect base address.

The NAPOTDecoder comment (line 918) explicitly documents the design assumption: '66 bit addr，{entry_addrh, entry_addr, 2'b11}' and line 929 states 'entry_addr = padding 01 (NA4)/ padding 11(NAPOT4)'. The examples (lines 936-943) all assume exactly 2-bit padding. This confirms the design was architected for G=2 only. The NAPOTDecoder itself correctly computes trailing-ones → mask → base/range, but it operates on an input that has been incorrectly padded for G>2. There is no HWCFG3/granularity register anywhere in the RTL (grep for 'granularity|hwcfg3|HWCFG3' returns zero results).

soc_addr_width is hardcoded to 48 at line 116, but io.entry.addr is 64 bits (to hold {entry_addrh[31:0], entry_addr[31:0]}). The 48-bit soc_addr_width cannot represent the full 64-bit entry address space when addrh_en=1. The consistent undersizing of soc_addr_width relative to the entry address register width suggests a deeper architectural mismatch: either soc_addr_width should be at least 64 when addrh is enabled, or the Cat(Cat(entry_addrh, entry_addr), 2-bit-pad) concatenation should not flow through a 48-bit bottleneck.
